source_read: PMC HTML (PMC5899998), full text read in my own browser tab: Summary, Introduction, Methods, Research in context panel, Results (7 paragraphs), Tables 1-2, Figure 1 viewed on screen (category hazard ratios read approximately from the plot), legends of Figures 2-4, Discussion, funding, contributors and declaration of interests; appendix not read. The article carries a correction notice (Lancet 2018;391:2212), not read.

claims.overstatement: Minor: (1) 'intake is mostly under-reported' does not come from this source, which says only that self-reported intake is prone to bias; (2) 'people who had cut down because of illness stayed in the lighter groups' is firmer than the source, which says such people were probably included and that reverse causation cannot be excluded. No 'safe' wording; the claim keeps the comparison inside people who drink (against light drinkers), which is what stops 'lowest below about 100 g a week' reading as a safe amount, and it should keep that framing.
claims.note: Numbers checked and matching: 83 studies, 19 high-income countries, 599,912 current drinkers without known cardiovascular disease, mean age 57, 40,310 deaths, median follow-up 7.5 years; reference group more than 0 and up to 25 g a week (Figure 1 legend); about 50% above 100 g a week, median 96 g; life expectancy at 40 about 6 months, 1-2 years and 4-5 years shorter against more than 0 to 100 g; men above 112 g 1.6 years (1.3-1.8), above 196 g 2.7 years (2.4-3.1); women above 112 or 98 g 1.3 years (1.1-1.5); per 100 g a week stroke 1.14 (1.10-1.17), heart failure 1.09 (1.03-1.15), fatal hypertensive disease 1.24 (1.15-1.33), fatal aortic aneurysm 1.15 (1.03-1.28), coronary disease other than myocardial infarction 1.06 (1.00-1.11), myocardial infarction 0.94 (0.91-0.97). Recomputed: 100 g a week = 14.3 g a day (about 14) and ten 10-g drinks; 45 g a day = 315 g a week; 25 g a day = 175 g a week: same. Points the claim could add: the hazard ratios are per 100 g a week of usual intake, corrected for within-person variation with 152,640 repeat measurements in 71,011 people from 37 studies (regression dilution ratio 0.50), and Figure 1 plots risk against usual intake, so 'usually once' describes the measurement, not the analysis. Read approximately from Figure 1, hazard ratios stay about 1.00 up to roughly 80 g a week of usual intake, are only about 1.02-1.03 in the two groups at roughly 105 and 150 g, and are clearly raised (about 1.2 and 1.45) in the two heaviest groups, so the excess just above 100 g a week is small. The main models adjusted only for age, smoking status (current or not) and diabetes, stratified by sex and study or centre; further adjustment (body-mass index, blood pressure, lipids, education, occupation and others) is said not to have changed results substantially, but values are shown only for cardiovascular outcomes (Table 2). Life expectancy is modelled by applying the hazard ratios to US death rates (CDC WONDER, 2007-10); about 20% of the men's survival difference came from cardiovascular deaths. 'Rose less steeply at older ages' and 'in men and women alike' rest on appendix figures cited in the text.

anchors.extracted: Of 786,787 eligible participants, 186,875 (19%) non-drinkers excluded, leaving 599,912 current drinkers without cardiovascular disease from 83 studies (ERFC 247,504, EPIC-CVD 26,036, UK Biobank 326,372) in 19 high-income countries, recruited 1964-2010; mean age 57 (SD 9), 44% women, 21% current smokers; about 50% drank more than 100 g a week, 8.4% more than 350 g; 5.4 million person-years, median follow-up 7.5 years; 40,310 deaths.

All-cause mortality: positive, curvilinear association, lowest risk below 100 g a week, similar in men and women, weaker at older ages; reference group more than 0 to 25 g a week; per 100 g a week of usual intake, stroke 1.14 (1.10-1.17), coronary disease excluding MI 1.06 (1.00-1.11), heart failure 1.09 (1.03-1.15), fatal hypertensive disease 1.24 (1.15-1.33), fatal aortic aneurysm 1.15 (1.03-1.28), MI 0.94 (0.91-0.97). Plot (approximate): HR about 1.0 up to about 80 g usual, about 1.02-1.03 near 105 and 150 g, about 1.2 near 210 g and 1.45 near 340 g.

anchors.locator: Results, 7th paragraph; Figure 4 legend; Methods > Statistical analysis, 5th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Against more than 0 to 100 g a week (mean usual 56 g), groups at more than 100-200 (123 g), 200-350 (208 g) and above 350 g (367 g) had about 6 months, 1-2 years and 4-5 years shorter life expectancy at 40; men above 112 g 1.6 years (1.3-1.8), above 196 g 2.7 years (2.4-3.1); women above 112 or 98 g about 1.3 years (1.1-1.5); modelled on US CDC WONDER death rates.

Baseline intake median 96 g a week (5th-95th percentiles 6-448); weakly correlated with male sex, smoking status and amount, systolic blood pressure, HDL-C, fibrinogen and lower socioeconomic status; regression dilution ratio for intake 0.50 (0.47-0.52).

Cox models within each study, stratified by sex, adjusted for age, smoking status (current or not) and history of diabetes, pooled by random-effects meta-analysis; usual intake estimated by regression calibration from 152,640 repeat measurements in 71,011 participants of 37 studies; hazard ratios refer to usual intake.

Self-reported intake prone to bias; no life-course data; people who cut down but did not stop because of ill health probably included, so reverse causation cannot be excluded; injuries, liver disease and psychiatric outcomes not available; randomised trials needed.

Further adjustment for other risk factors did not substantially change hazard ratios (exceptions for HDL-C and blood pressure in cardiovascular subtypes; Table 2 shows cardiovascular outcomes only); in exploratory analyses beer or spirits, less frequent and binge drinking had stronger associations with death but went with more smoking and lower socioeconomic status.

claims.note: The statement does not cite this source; it qualifies the comparison-group argument. The main text gives no estimates against non-drinkers; the U shape with non-drinkers included is described with values only in the appendix (not read).

anchors.extracted: With never-drinkers and ex-drinkers included, the previously reported U-shaped associations with all-cause mortality and total cardiovascular disease were reproduced (appendix); never-drinkers differed from current drinkers at baseline in sex, ethnicity, smoking and diabetes.

anchors.locator: Methods > Study design, data sources, and participants, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Analysis restricted to current drinkers because ex-drinkers include people who stopped because of poor health and never-drinkers may differ from drinkers in ways that are hard to measure.

key_findings.correction: Arithmetic recomputed: 599,912 + 186,875 = 786,787 exactly, so the 786,787 are current drinkers plus non-drinkers, and 186,875 of them is 23.75%, not the printed 19%.
Recomputed from Table 1: 52,429 of 599,912 above the top cut-off = 8.74%; 293,862 above 100 g a week = 49.0% ('about 50%').
Figure 1 can be read approximately on screen (see missed).
Binge drinking defined as 100 g or more per occasion in Methods > Statistical analysis, 3rd paragraph.
Checked on PMC (PMC5986662): only Makoto Daimon's affiliation corrected (online version corrected 31 May 2018).

reporting_issues.note: 12,090 + 14,539 + 7,990 = 34,619; with heart failure and other CVD deaths 38,451; Table 1's 'All cardiovascular disease' row does sum to 39,018 (18,791 + 12,758 + 7,469).
The plotted values can be read approximately from the image (about 1.02-1.03 just above 100 g a week, about 1.2 and 1.45 in the two heaviest groups), but not quoted as numbers.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E overall high agrees: main models adjust only for age, smoking status and diabetes (stratified by sex), further adjustment is reported in words or only for cardiovascular outcomes, and residual reverse causation is conceded. Domain judgments agree.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is defensible because the abstract restricts its conclusion to current drinkers in high-income countries, but it is at the upper edge: the Discussion's first paragraph presents a long-term reduction from 196 to 100 g a week as associated with 1-2 years longer life, a within-person change the study did not observe.

missed: Reporting inconsistency on the life-expectancy method: Methods > Statistical analysis, 5th paragraph says age-at-risk HRs for cause-specific mortality were applied to CDC WONDER rates, while the Figure 4 legend says HRs for all-cause mortality by baseline category were applied to US death rates; the Results' attribution of about 20% of the men's survival difference to cardiovascular deaths fits the cause-specific version.

Figure 1, read approximately on screen by this reader: HRs about 1.00 for the categories up to about 80 g a week of usual intake, about 1.02 and 1.03 at about 105 and 150 g, about 1.2 at about 210 g and about 1.45 at about 340 g; so the excess just above 100 g a week is small and the clear rise is in the two heaviest groups. Approximate only; exact values are in the appendix.

Figure 1 and the per-100 g HRs are on the usual-intake scale (regression-calibrated), while the life-expectancy groups are defined by reported baseline intake (mean usual 56, 123, 208 and 367 g); claims giving '100 g a week' should not mix the two scales without saying so.
